cells.tense: The first clear look is here and you are in it, taking it in as it comes, with the pen in your hand.
cells.ask: Name the pull you can actually see — the real one, not the loudest — and follow it one step further than is comfortable.
cells.core:
You are seeing the direction and you are pointed at it. Not chasing every flash that moves, not squinting past the one that holds — you can tell which pull is yours and you let it aim you. That sorting runs every day, steady, and you would be within your rights to lean on it more.

What this balance is free to feed next is reach: say the pull out loud to one person who would take it seriously. Naming the one you can actually see — the real one, not the loudest — and walking it one step past comfortable is how seeing turns into a road instead of a feeling.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the direction and you're pointed at it.
cells.verb: Seeing freshly before the seeing has anything to grab
cells.place: where the pull toward what you actually want lives

cells.tense: You are braced for a light that hasn't arrived, writing into a future that can't be scripted yet.
cells.ask: When you want an idea to move toward you, take one plain step and leave the rest unplanned.
cells.core:
You keep glimpsing the next clarity before it's ready and trying to live in it now. Every version of the far shore gets compared, tested, rehearsed — and the bracing is doing more steering than the direction is. The push to be already there is exactly what keeps you from following the light you're actually under.

What closes the gap is movement without a script. Pick an idea you want to walk toward and take one plain step toward it, leaving the rest of the plan blank on purpose. Letting it progress through your own action, today, in unplanned shape, is how the future stops being something you brace against.
cells.sheetLine: You're living in a next light that's already costing you this one.
cells.verb: Seeing freshly before the seeing has anything to grab
cells.place: where the pull toward what you actually want lives

cells.tense: You are standing at a door already behind you, still looking back instead of at the light that is here.
cells.ask: Build one small, finished piece of the thing you can see — a first version, done, and kept.
cells.core:
When this is working, you can point at your direction and walk under it without checking behind you. The pull is clear enough to move by, and you let it lead you through the day in small steps. Seeing is enough; the walking follows on its own when the eye is steady.

What has gone quiet is the walking. You still see where the light is, and you have stopped moving toward it. The pointing is all that's left of the practice — the road under the need has gone unused.

What restores movement is finishing something. Pick one small piece of what you can see and carry it all the way to done — a first version, kept. Completing a form through steady effort is what puts the road back under the light.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the direction and you aren't steering by it.
cells.verb: Seeing freshly before the seeing has anything to grab
cells.place: where the pull toward what you actually want lives

cells.tense: The pen is down, the writing is running, and you are talking about the light as if it were out of your hands.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, that the light you've been following is yours — that you're the one steering by it.
cells.core:
You are already oriented, already pointed, already living toward something bright — and you tell it as if the pull came from somewhere else. The steering is happening every day; the owning of it isn't. What's missing isn't the light and isn't the seeing. It's the claim on the seeing.

The quieter form of this is confidence in your own sight, not more description of it. Say out loud, once, that the light is yours — that you are the one steering by it — and let the claim land without taking it back. That returns seeing to its simplest face: light shining because it is light, and the one standing in it owns the shining.
cells.sheetLine: You're already steering by a light you call someone else's.
